author: Amphilochius of Iconium
addressee: A Christian congregation assembled for the Holy Saturday liturgy
occasion: A festal homily delivered on Holy Saturday, celebrating Christ's burial and anticipating his resurrection, while answering Jewish and pagan mockery of the Christian hope.
argument: Amphilochius contrasts the apparent triumph of death over Christ with the hidden reality that death has swallowed life itself and will be despoiled. He recalls the cosmic signs at the crucifixion and the paradoxes of the Creator suffering at human hands, all endured willingly and with forgiving love. Turning to the Jews who sealed and guarded the tomb, he argues that their very precautions betray their fear that Jesus was no mere man, and he challenges them to await the third day. He closes by invoking the raising of Lazarus as proof of Christ's power, laments Jewish blindness, and invites the faithful to join the women at the tomb in faith, ending with a doxology.

outline.move: The homily opens by celebrating the burial feast of the Saviour, contrasting Christ's descent to despoil Hades with the Church's joyful anticipation of resurrection, and noting the mockery of Jews and Greeks.
The preacher recalls the cosmic upheaval at the crucifixion and the paradoxes of the Creator suffering, emphasizing Christ's willing endurance and prayer for his crucifiers.
He taunts the Jews for guarding a dead man, arguing that their fear and precautions prove they do not believe Jesus was a mere human, and urges them to stop fighting against God and truth.

He insists that resurrection cannot be hindered by weapons, seals, or guards, points to Lazarus as proof, laments Jewish blindness, and invites the faithful to join the women at the tomb, ending with a doxology.

cast.name: Jews
cast.who: The opponents who crucified Christ, sealed his tomb, and set guards, yet fear his resurrection.

cast.name: Greeks
cast.who: Pagans who mock the Christian hope and have shut up their hopes in tombs.

cast.name: Lazarus
cast.who: The man Christ raised from the dead, cited as proof of his power over death.

key_terms.sense: The realm of the dead, which Christ enters to despoil and fill with light
Christ's rising from the dead, the central hope of the feast
Death personified as an enemy who seizes Christ but cannot hold him
Corruption or decay, which the holy one will not experience
A mere human being, the category the Jews implicitly deny by guarding the tomb
The temple of Jerusalem, whose veil was torn at the crucifixion; also Christ's body in the saying quoted
The seal placed on the tomb, which cannot hinder the resurrection
Those who killed Christ, for whom he prays and intercedes
The unbelief of the Jews, which blinds them to the truth
Life personified, which death has swallowed but cannot retain

scripture: The author quotes the Psalms according to the Septuagint numbering (e.g. Psalm 15:10 'You will not give your holy one to see corruption'; Psalm 48:12 'Their tombs are their houses forever'). He also quotes Isaiah 9:2 ('the people sitting in darkness have seen a great light'), the Gospel of John 2:19 ('Destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it'), Luke 23:34 ('Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do'), John 11:43 ('Come out'), and John 20:2 ('They have taken away my Lord and I do not know where they have laid him'), adapted to the plural for the congregation. The passage 'They have eyes but do not see, ears have they and do not hear' alludes to Isaiah 6:9-10, and 'the god of this age has blinded their minds' matches 2 Corinthians 4:4. Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names and Hebrew Psalm numbering where it differs from the Septuagint.

_unresolved_facts.fix: John 20:13/20:2 ('They have taken away my Lord and I do not know where they have laid him'), adapted to the plural for the congregation. The exact form Ἦραν ἡμῶν τὸν κύριον καὶ οὐκ οἴδαμεν τί ἐποίησαν αὐτόν matches John 20:13 (Mary Magdalene's words to the angels) more closely than John 20:2, though both verses are similar.
